lead: The instrument cluster is the small computer sitting in front of the driver. It receives frames from other ECUs on the CAN bus and pulses from sensors wired to it directly, then turns that data into a needle angle, a digit, a warning lamp or an image floating on the windscreen. It exists because the driver must read speed, engine speed, fuel, temperature and faults in one glance without looking away from the road. Every car, bus and truck on an Indian road has one.
prereq: You need: CAN frames from Unit 6, CAN and CAN FD protocols and wheel-speed sensing from Unit 3, crankshaft position and engine speed sensors.

sections.h3: The cluster as a node on the bus

blocks.text: Behind the dashboard sits a small computer with its own microcontroller, memory and display driver. It is a node on the CAN bus. It reads frames from the engine ECU, the ABS ECU and the body controller, and it also reads a few sensors wired to it directly, such as the fuel-level float.

The cluster drives four things: stepper motors that move the needles, an LCD or TFT panel, LED telltales and the backlight. The main gauges are the speedometer in km/h, the tachometer in rpm (shown in thousands), the fuel gauge from E to F, and the coolant temperature gauge from C to H. The odometer is not a gauge; it is a stored count of distance held in the cluster's memory.

Telltales use fixed colours. Red means stop — low oil pressure, brake fault, handbrake on. Amber means caution — check engine, ABS, low fuel. Green and blue mean status — indicators, high beam. The driver information display adds the trip meter, range, outside temperature and door-open warnings.

The cluster also stores diagnostic trouble codes and lights a lamp when one is set; a scan tool reads the full code. At key-on it runs a self-test: every telltale lights, and every needle sweeps full scale and back. A needle that does not sweep has a failed motor or driver.

The speedometer does not use engine rpm. A sensor at the gearbox output or at each wheel sends one electrical pulse for every tooth or magnet that passes it. The number of pulses per kilometre, K, is a constant stored in the cluster for a given tyre and sensor.

The distance per pulse is d = C / N metres, where C is the tyre rolling circumference in metres and N is the number of pulses per wheel revolution. Equivalently, d = 1000 / K when K is in pulses per km.
The cluster counts n whole pulses in a fixed window of T seconds, then computes the speed.

blocks.where: v is speed in km/h; n is the number of pulses counted in the window; d is the distance per pulse in metres; T is the window length in seconds; 3.6 converts m/s to km/h.

blocks.text: A short window reacts quickly but is coarse at low speed, because few pulses arrive. A long window is smooth but lags. Many clusters use a longer window below about 30 km/h, or measure the time between pulses instead. Tyre wear, pressure, load and a change of tyre size all change C, so the reading drifts. The same wheel-speed pulses feed the ABS and ESP, which is why one faulty wheel sensor can light the ABS lamp and disturb the speedometer together.

sections.h3: Needles, panels and the head-up display

blocks.text: A modern needle is driven by a small stepper motor through a reduction gear. The driver chip sends a number of steps, not a voltage, so the cluster can command any angle repeatably. The motor holds its position by magnetic detent when power is removed. Older clusters used a crossed-coil movement, where two coils at right angles pulled a magnet and the needle angle depended on the ratio of their currents.

A segmented LCD shows fixed digits cheaply. A dot-matrix LCD or a colour TFT gives free-form text, menus, a reversing camera image or a map. The backlight is a string of white LEDs, dimmed by pulse-width modulation. The dimming command comes from a light sensor on the dash, the headlamp switch, or a button the driver presses; on the bus it is a short CAN frame.

A head-up display (HUD) throws light from a projector in the dash onto a combiner — a small glass screen above the cluster — or onto a special wedge-shaped layer inside the windscreen. The driver sees a virtual image that appears to float ahead of the car.

Virtual image distance is how far ahead the image seems to be. For a windscreen HUD it is typically 2 to 2.5 m in front of the driver's eye. The image is deliberately focused far, not at the glass. A driver looking at the road is focused at 20 m or more. If the HUD image sat at 0.5 m, the eye would have to re-focus and converge for near vision on every glance, taking about 0.2 s and losing the road picture. At 2.5 m the eye stays almost at road focus. The HUD shows speed, the speed limit, a navigation arrow and ADAS warnings — short items read in one glance, not maps. Brightness must follow daylight; too bright at night causes glare.

figure.caption: The wheel sensor and engine ECU feed the cluster; the cluster drives the needle and the head-up image; the driver's dimming command returns. Notice the two different inputs: a raw pulse train for speed and a bus frame for engine speed.

spec.aria: Sequence over time: the wheel sensor sends 58 pulses per second and the engine ECU sends a CAN frame with 3000 rpm to the cluster; the cluster shows a needle at 100 km/h and a head-up image at 2.5 m to the driver; the driver sends a dimming command back to the cluster.

examples.question: A speedometer receives N = 4 pulses per wheel revolution. The tyre rolling circumference is C = 1.90 m. The cluster counts whole pulses in a window of T = 0.5 s. Find (a) the distance per pulse, (b) the pulse frequency at 100 km/h, (c) the number of pulses counted in one window, and (d) the speed the cluster displays from that count.
steps: Distance per pulse: d = C / N = 1.90 / 4 = 0.475 m per pulse.
Convert the true speed: 100 km/h = 100 / 3.6 = 27.78 m/s.
Pulses in T = 0.5 s: n = 58.48 × 0.5 = 29.24. The counter keeps whole pulses, so n = 29.
examples.answer: d = 0.475 m, f = 58.48 pulses/s, count = 29, displayed speed = 99.18 km/h — about 0.8 km/h low because the fractional pulse is dropped.
examples.check:
circ = 1.90
ppr = 4
v_kmh = 100.0
d = circ / ppr
print(round(d, 3))
v = v_kmh / 3.6
rev = v / circ
f = rev * ppr
print(round(f, 2))
n = f * 0.5
print(round(n, 2))
counted = int(n)
print(counted)
displayed = 3.6 * counted * d / 0.5
print(round(displayed, 2))

traps: Thinking the speedometer is driven by engine rpm. It is driven by wheel or gearbox pulses, so a change of tyre size or final drive changes the reading.
Mixing pulses per kilometre with pulses per revolution. K is per km, N is per wheel turn; convert between them with the rolling circumference.
Dropping the factor 3.6 between m/s and km/h, which makes the answer 3.6 times wrong.
Using the tyre's nominal radius instead of the loaded rolling circumference. Load and pressure change it, and that changes the stored distance per pulse.
Forgetting that the cluster counts whole pulses. The window value rounds down, so the displayed speed is slightly low; averaging several windows or timing the pulse period removes the error.

quiz.q: Name four gauges on a typical instrument cluster and give the unit of each.
quiz.a: Speedometer in km/h, tachometer in rpm (shown in thousands), fuel gauge from E to F with no unit, coolant temperature gauge in °C marked C to H.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a red and an amber telltale?
quiz.a: Red means stop now — a safety fault such as low oil pressure or a brake fault. Amber means caution — a fault to check soon, such as check engine or ABS.

quiz.q: Why does the cluster sweep every needle at key-on?
quiz.a: It is a self-test. A full-scale sweep proves the stepper motor, its driver and its return detent work. A needle that does not move points to a failed motor or driver before the car moves.

quiz.q: A sensor gives K = 8000 pulses per kilometre. Find the distance per pulse.
A wheel of rolling circumference 2.0 m turns at 72 km/h with 4 pulses per revolution. Find the pulse frequency.
quiz.a: 72 km/h = 20 m/s. Revolutions per second = 20 / 2.0 = 10. f = 10 × 4 = 40 pulses/s.

quiz.q: A car reads 5% high after fitting smaller tyres. Explain using pulses per kilometre.
quiz.a: Smaller tyres have a smaller rolling circumference, so the car covers more wheel revolutions per km and K rises. The cluster still uses the old, larger distance per pulse, so each counted pulse is credited with too much distance and the speed reads high. Re-entering the correct K or tyre-size code fixes it.

quiz.q: Why is the HUD virtual image placed about 2.5 m ahead rather than at the windscreen surface?
quiz.a: The driver's eye is focused far down the road. An image at 0.5 m forces accommodation and convergence for near vision on every glance, costing about 0.2 s of re-focus. At 2.5 m the eye stays near road focus, so speed is read in one glance without losing the road.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production clusters are merging into one large TFT driven by a domain controller, and the HUD is moving to augmented reality, drawing navigation arrows on the lane ahead. Engineers work on legibility in strong Indian sunlight, plastic combiner optics and the functional safety of telltales. Search for automotive head-up display virtual image distance, cluster stepper motor driver, and in-vehicle display ergonomics.
